quote: Wo fängt Mathem. an? III S. 116
english: Where does mathematics begin? (notebook III, p. 116)
topic: An index-like list of notes with page references to notebook III on the foundations of mathematics: proper functions, an axiom that every equation has a root, axiom layers as rings, provability with or without the Archimedean axiom, where mathematics begins, consistency as existence, and a defence against Frege.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a mathematical research question. It is a foundational and philosophical one: what is the starting point of mathematics, and does it come before logic or depend on it? It is the logicism question (Frege/Dedekind: arithmetic is reducible to logic), and the same index line contains a 'defence against Frege'. In modern terms: is arithmetic based on pure logic (logicism), or should logic and arithmetic be built up together from concrete, finite symbols, with consistency playing the role of existence? The diary entry is only an index pointer to notebook III, p. 116, which I have not seen, so its exact content cannot be checked.
triage.answered_by: No mathematical answer is possible. Hilbert gave his own philosophical answer in public. In his 1904 Heidelberg ICM talk (published 1905) he rejected Frege's and Dedekind's foundations and proposed developing logic and arithmetic simultaneously. From 1922 on, his finitary standpoint said mathematics begins with concrete signs that are intuitively present before all thought ('Über das Unendliche', 1925/26). Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) are widely taken to show that the full Hilbert program cannot be carried out. The underlying philosophical question has not been settled.

evidence.claim: In the 1904 Heidelberg talk Hilbert called the foundations of Frege and Dedekind flawed by contradictions and sketched a proof-theoretic program.
Hilbert first proposed in 1905 that mathematics and logic be developed simultaneously, and he later followed that plan with Bernays.
From 1922 on, Hilbert's finitary standpoint restricted mathematical thought to concrete extra-logical discrete objects that exist intuitively before all thought, meaning a basis of concrete signs.
In 'On the Infinite', Hilbert puts the starting point in extralogical concrete objects that are intuited as directly experienced.
It is widely (though not universally) accepted that Hilbert's program cannot be carried out, because of Gödel's results.

triage.why: The line asks a philosophy-of-mathematics question, not a statement that could be proved or disproved. It sits next to 'consistency as existence' and 'defence against Frege', which fits Hilbert's anti-logicist position from around 1904–05 and his later finitism. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Debate about the foundations of mathematics continues in philosophy, but sources do not treat this line as a distinct research problem. Confidence is medium because I could not see notebook III, p. 116, and the sources do not mention this diary entry, so linking it to Hilbert's published views is an inference.
